finding: Nested reference/expression superscripts and derivative notation can be confused. Rotating a zero B-relative velocity does not produce its generally nonzero A-relative motion.
handling: Name the differentiation observer and expression basis separately. Add transport terms only when changing the physical observer.

finding: The diagram labels successive geometric vectors even though the point is fixed in its body frame. Their directions in the fixed frame change, but the body-coordinate tuple remains constant.
handling: Interpret the picture geometrically in fixed frame A; do not subtract coordinate tuples expressed in different moving bases.

finding: The small-motion equation uses radius times angle for displacement length. A finite tip chord differs from the circular arc; the intermediate scalar/vector notation is compressed.
handling: Use the infinitesimal limit or an explicitly first-order approximation. The exact instantaneous vector result is omega×r.

finding: The revolute linear recurrence assumes the parent-to-child origin offset is constant in the parent frame and the new joint axis passes through the child origin.
handling: Preserve that frame placement. Do not apply the formula unchanged to arbitrary frame choices or an offset tool point.

finding: The printed most-general 6×6 claim conflicts with the nonsquare statement and later 6×n summary. Mandatory time variation is also too broad.
handling: Use 6×n for the full spatial task with n joint-rate inputs; 6×6 is the n=6 case. Configuration-induced time variation can vanish.

finding: Blockdiag(R,R) changes the expression basis of the same point/body velocity. It does not include a physical reference-point shift or change of moving observer.
handling: Keep the same physical point and observer. A point shift requires the appropriate omega×r term. The source equation is valid within its proper scope.

finding: The descriptions of losing one Cartesian coordinate and requiring infinite motion at the actual singularity are overbroad.
handling: Use task-rank loss; unavailable directions can combine named axes. Near-singular inverse mapping may amplify rates. At exact rank loss, compatible targets may have finite solutions while incompatible targets have no exact solution.

finding: Joint-axis alignment and workspace-edge examples are context dependent. Claims about additional singularities and singularity-free structures need task/model bounds.
handling: Use the correct task-map rank test. Joint limits can bound a workspace without differential rank loss, and duplicate columns need not eliminate full row rank in a redundant task. Treat other failure modes separately.

finding: The explicit-Jacobian safety claim and the RL/RMRC behavioral connection are not qualified on the slide.
handling: Treat the RL connection as an analogy. Interpretability alone does not guarantee safety without explicit constraints, valid models and controller checks.

finding: Enlarged PDF pixels make combining overdots overlap the theta glyph. Encoded PDF text contains U+0307 on the computed rate and Euler-rate factor; the same rendering issue occurs on p323.
handling: Do not label these as missing-dot source equations. Transcribe theta_dot explicitly and retain the rejected defect allegation.

finding: Exact analytic-model and neural-inverse wording can be overread. Learning derivatives are not necessarily the robot’s geometric Jacobian; named software examples are not current-API guarantees.
handling: Use conditional model fidelity and source-attributed examples. Do not claim every neural IK map equals the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse or every model-free RL method uses an analytic robot Jacobian.

finding: The summary introduces a 6×n Jacobian and then uses det J=0 without restricting the matrix to square dimensions.
handling: Use an ordinary determinant only for square matrices; otherwise use task rank. Force-transpose questions state their virtual-power scope and do not claim to model all robot dynamics.
